Dagda.json.text: The Dagda is an ancient Irish god of the Tuatha Dé Danann. His common title is "the good god", because he is good at many things at once. Koch 2006 derives his name from a Celtic compound meaning excellence and god, and tradition usually calls him the Dagda with the definite article. His alternative names include Eochaid Ollathair, understood as all-father or great father, together with the byname Ruad Rofhessa. The name Eochaid Ollathair invites comparison with the Norse god Óðinn, who is similarly versatile. He works as artisan, diviner, husbandman, warrior, and wise king. He is also benevolent and rules over abundance and fertility. The Dagda owns a cauldron that never empties. He drags a huge mallet behind him on a cart, and Koch 2006 describes a club that deals death to the living and restores the dead, so enormous that wheels are needed to move it. He keeps pigs that can be eaten again and again, each time reviving themselves. He holds an orchard that always bears fruit, in any season. Koch 2006 treats him as a transfunctional deity who joins craft wisdom to the passage between death and renewal. The fullest surviving description of him occurs in the great tale Cath Maige Tuired. His usual guise is gross and uncouth. Sent to the enemy camp in that tale, the Fomoiri make sport of him and compel him to gulp a vast bowl of porridge that has been tipped into a pit in the dirt. Such is his greed that he eats every last spoonful and wipes the hollow clean with his finger, yet he still manages to seduce the daughter of his enemy and so secure victory for his own people. Scholars compare his many roles with those of the Gaulish Sucellus and of Heracles, and in the Dumézilian scheme he stands for the third function, the provision of wealth and food. He has also been identified with Donn and Dis Pater as a god of the Otherworld. His usual consort is Bóand, and their children include Brigit and Aonghus óg, whom Koch 2006 names as Oengus Mac ind Óc. He also fathers the fairy king Midir, the magician Bodb Derg, and other children of the Mythological Cycle, including Áed Menbhrec, Cermat, and Ainge. He mates with many goddesses, including the Mórrígan at the River Unshin, who agrees to back his side at Mag Tuired. At the second battle Cethlion, wife of Balor, kills him. He then reigns from the otherworld, still fed by his cauldron and orchard. His seat is at Brú na Bóinne, the great earthworks on the Boyne. He buries his slain son Áed Minbhrec at Grianán Aileach, in modern County Donegal.

Deirdre.json.text: Deirdre (also Derdriu or Deridriu) was an Irish heroine. People called her "Deirdre of the Sorrows." Her story ranks with the two other great sorrows of Ireland, the Children of Lir and the Sons of Tuireann. Koch 2006 records her as the beautiful daughter of the storyteller Feidlimid mac Daill, and as the focus of a tragic love triangle with the young hero Noísiu mac Uislenn, with Conchobar the ruler of Ulaid. Koch also explains her name in Longas mac nUislenn, where the druid Cathbad hears the unborn girl cry out in the womb and takes her cry for a portent, a verb otherwise unattested that probably relates to the Old Irish words for noise and murmuring. Her story was born during a feast. Her father Fedlimid mac Daill held the feast for Concobar mac Nessa, king of Ulster. The druid Cathbad foretold her fate. She would grow into a woman of unmatched beauty, he said, without equal in Ireland. Her beauty would destroy the kingdom. Concobar chose to rear her as his prize. He gave her to Leborcham at Emain Macha. One day Deirdre saw a raven feeding on a calf's blood spread over fresh snow. She wanted a man with hair like the raven, skin like snow, and lips like blood. That man was Noísiu, son of Uisneach and a nephew of the king. Deirdre and Noísiu fled with his brothers Ardán and Ainnle. They crossed to Scotland and lived near Loch Etive. Concobar lured them back to Ireland. On landing, Noísiu and his brothers were killed. Deirdre reproached the king for the deed. Koch 2006 places the earliest surviving version of her story in the Old Irish saga Longas Mac nUislenn, the tale of how the sons of Uisliu went into exile, and he counts her fate among the three great sorrows of Irish storytelling, which the Children of Lir and the Sons of Tuireann share with her. He compares her unhappy love with that of Gráinne and Diarmaid, of Tristan and Isolt, and of the Galatian priestess Camma. The tale stayed popular in the Gaelic world, and Koch 2006 credits this popularity with the widespread use of the name Deirdre today. J. M. Synge, writing in English, staged his version of Deirdre of the Sorrows in 1910, and Alexander Carmichael published an oral Scottish Gaelic telling of the tale.

Dindshenchas.json.text: Dindshenchas is an Irish mythological text. The name means lore of high places, and later usage writes it dinnsheanchas. These texts describe myths tied to places in the landscape, showing how a river, hill, fort, or plain received its name. The poems form a body of place-lore. Koch 2006 explains that part of the lore grew directly out of mythology, such as the catalogue of landscape features found at the close of Táin Bó Cuailnge, born from the fatal duel of two supernatural bulls. In an earlier scene the hero Cú Chulainn, standing on a hill, has his charioteer name the chief forts he can see between Tara and Kells. Such a triangulation of Ireland mattered to a society that needed to know where one local kingdom, or tuath, ended and its neighbour began, since ordinary people lost legal protection outside their own territory. Hills often marked those boundaries, and people chose them for ritual and assembly. Poets who had finished eight years of training were expected to narrate the traditional stories and say how each place had come by its name. Koch 2006 names Mac Liacc, Cinaed ua hArtacáin, and Cúán ua Lothcháin as authors of dindshenchas poems, and notes that an 11th-century compilation shows up in many important Irish manuscripts. Edward Gwynn edited the metrical version in five volumes, and Whitley Stokes edited anonymous prose pieces from different collections. The later editions were planned to hold verse and prose together. Koch 2006 observes that the stories often touch the mythological tradition and the folk of the síd, that references to the Ulster sagas and to the tales of Finn mac Cumaill outnumber those to the Kings' Cycle, and that a few saints appear in them, among them Colum Cille and Patrick. Many poems end with religious stanzas that praise the coming of Christianity. Place-name stories kept circulating in Irish oral lore into the modern era. The date of the earliest form is unknown, and the Dindshenchas may have been recited aloud long before the twelfth-century Book of Leinster and other medieval manuscripts gave it written form. Many ancient Irish stories reach us only through this text.

Dôn.json.text: Dôn was a Welsh mythological ancestress, largely unknown in her own right. The gods of Wales carried her name as the Children of Dôn, in Welsh Plant Dôn. Koch 2006 records her as the mother of three central characters of the Middle Welsh tale Math fab Mathonwy, which forms the fourth main tale of the Mabinogi: Arianrhod, Gilfaethwy, and Gwydion. Culhwch ac Olwen names her as the mother of Amaethon mab Don, a supernatural ploughman, and of Gouannon mab Don, a supernatural smith. An early 11th-century Breton Life of Saint Iudic-hael makes the legendary poet Taliesin a son of Dôn, and the genealogies of the Hanesyn Hen tract localize her progeny in north Wales as Plant Don o Arvon. Koch 2006 keeps her separate from the Irish goddess Danu, arguing that the usual equation of Dôn with the Tuatha Dé Danann and with the Danube is phonetically unworkable, since a cognate of Middle Irish Danu in British would necessarily give Welsh forms such as Dyn or Dein. He notes that scholars have doubted how old and genuine Middle Irish Danu truly is, and that another proposed etymology reads Dôn as a cognate of the Old Irish word don, meaning place, ground, or earth, and so as a parallel to the Greek khthōn. Welsh Dôn occurs only as a semantic genitive, usually preceded by merch, daughter, mab, son, or plant, children. Plant Dôn, the Children of the Earth, would then match the children of Llŷr, whose name belongs with the sea, and the Titans of Hesiod, primeval beings born of the earth. Her daughter Arianrhod once stood as a footstool before Math, Dôn's brother and king. Dôn had four sons, and three of them held social roles: the bard Gwydion, the smith Govannon, and the farmer Amaethon. The fourth, Gilfaethwy, was a trickster. The Children of Dôn inherited through the maternal line. Math passed rule to his nephew Gwydion, and Gwydion to Arianrhod's son Lleu Llaw Gyffes.
